studies.title: What To Do With Victory
studies.meaning: Three lines that describe a moment and then say what to do in it. Help and an opening arrive, people enter in crowds, and what follows is not celebration. The instructions are praise and asking pardon, which is what a person does after a fault, placed here after a success. The last clause gives the reason with a name of God in an intensive form, one who repeatedly turns back toward people.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources place it near the end of the mission, after Mecca had opened. Envoys were arriving from across Arabia. Several reports say the companions read it as a sign that the mission was ending, and that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) died not long after. The reports differ on details but agree on the reading.

keyTerms.note: A plural for groups arriving one after another, used of delegations and of troops. It describes the manner of entry rather than the number, so what is being noticed is the pace.
Two acts joined: declaring God free of any fault, and praising Him for what He has. The pair is a formula, and the first half is a denial before the second half affirms anything.
An intensive form of the verb used for a person's repentance, applied here to God. When He is the subject the sense is turning toward and accepting, and the intensive says He does it again and again.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: After Mecca opened, delegations came to Medina from tribes all across the peninsula. They arrived in groups, with their own questions and their own terms. Two decades earlier the community had been a few dozen people under threat. Now it was receiving envoys. Anyone who had been there from the start would have found the traffic outside the mosque hard to believe.
studies.didYouKnow: An early report describes a gathering in which senior companions were asked what this surah meant, and most spoke about victory. One of the youngest present said it was the announcement of the Prophet's death, and the man who had asked agreed with him. The surah says nothing about death directly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction is the surprising part. At the moment of greatest success, what is asked for is asking pardon. That puts a danger exactly where nobody looks for one. Victory is treated as an occasion to examine yourself, not to claim credit. The name of God that closes the surah then makes the asking natural rather than anxious. The one being asked is described as turning toward people again and again.

crossReferences.why: Names the same opening earlier and joins it to forgiveness in the same way, before the event.
Gives the same pairing of certainty and asking pardon, addressed to the same person mid-mission.
Marks the same closing period from another angle, the message described as finished rather than growing.

studies.applyIt: The next time something goes well for you, do what this surah asks. Before telling anyone, ask forgiveness once. Not for anything in particular. The instruction is placed at a success rather than at a failure. The practice is meant to break into the moment when a person is most likely to start taking credit.
studies.explainEasier: God says that when his help comes, and the city opens, people will join his religion in crowds. Then the messenger should praise his Lord and ask him for pardon. God takes people back when they turn to him.
